claim: Ccr5-/- mice showed enhanced contextual memory when tested 24 hr after training compared to WT mice.
source: The CCR5 knockout resulted in memory enhancements for contextual conditioning when tested 24 hr after training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, t(14) = 2.43 p<0.05, Student's t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of behavioral data comparing Ccr5-/- mice to WT mice in contextual fear conditioning.

claim: Ccr5-/- mice showed enhanced contextual memory when tested 2 weeks after training compared to WT mice.
source: The CCR5 knockout resulted in memory enhancements for contextual conditioning when tested 24 hr after training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, t(14) = 2.43 p<0.05, Student's t-test) and 2-weeks after training (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, t(14) = 3.07 p<0.01, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) of behavioral data comparing Ccr5-/- mice to WT mice in contextual fear conditioning at 2 weeks.

claim: The enhanced freezing of Ccr5-/- mice is not due to decreases in activity or increased sensitivity to the unconditioning stimulus.
source: Importantly, activity levels including baseline activity and activity bursts during shock-exposure were normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D), a result demonstrating that the enhanced freezing of Ccr5-/- mice is not due to either decreases in activity or increased sensitivity to the unconditioning stimulus (i.e., the footshock).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no differences in baseline activity and shock-induced activity bursts between Ccr5-/- and WT mice.

claim: Tone conditioning was unaltered in Ccr5-/- mice.
source: In contrast to contextual conditioning, tone conditioning (Hall et al., 2001) was unaltered in the Ccr5-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), confirming that the contextual conditioning enhancement of these mutants is not due to non-specific behavioral changes that alter conditioning responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing no difference in tone conditioning between Ccr5-/- and WT mice, and cites a reference for the tone conditioning method.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed increased freezing levels in contextual fear conditioning tested 2 weeks after training compared to WT littermates.
source: Compared to WT littermates, Ccr5+/- mice showed increased freezing levels (Figure 1A, t(20) = 2.37 p<0.05, Student's t-test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of behavioral data and reference to Figure 1A showing the results.

claim: Baseline activity and shock sensitivity were normal in Ccr5+/- mice.
source: in contrast, baseline activity and shock sensitivity were normal in these mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), demonstrating that both the Ccr5 heterozygous and homozygous mutations result in enhanced contextual memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no differences in baseline activity and shock sensitivity between Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice spent significantly more time in the target quadrant than in the other three quadrants of the water maze after two days of training.
source: In contrast, even with this limited amount of training, Ccr5+/- mice spent significantly more time in the quadrant where the platform had been during training (target quadrant) than the other three quadrants, demonstrating that the Ccr5+/- mutation not only enhances learning and memory for contextual conditioning, but also results in enhanced spatial learning and memory [Figure 1B; Two-way ANOVA with repeated measure, overall (genotype × percentage of time in each quadrant) interaction: F(3,84) = 0.81; Main effect of quadrant%: F(3,84) = 6.99. Between the target quadrant and all other quadrants for Ccr5+/- mice: p<0.05, Bonferroni post-tests].
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests, p<0.05) of water maze probe test data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: WT mice did not search selectively for the platform in the water maze probe test after two days of training.
source: Since this probe test was administered early in training, the WT mice did not search selectively for the platform.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations during the water maze probe test.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the novel OVX mouse in the social recognition test compared to WT mice.
source: In the test session, compared to WT mice, Ccr5+/- mice spent significantly more time exploring the novel OVX mouse, indicating that the Ccr5+/- mutation also enhanced learning and memory in the social recognition test (Figure 1C, t(18) = 3.39 p<0.01, one sample paired t-test compared to 50%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (one sample paired t-test, p<0.01) of social recognition test data and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The Ccr5+/- mutation did not affect the total interaction time during training in the social recognition test.
source: Importantly, the Ccr5+/- mutation did not affect the total interaction time during training, demonstrating that their learning and memory enhancement is not due to increased social interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing no difference in total interaction time during training between Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice were similar to WT littermates in both open arm entries and percentage time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus-maze.
source: Ccr5+/- mice were similar to WT littermates in both open arm entries and percentage time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus-maze, two well-known measures of anxiety (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the elevated plus-maze test and cites that these are well-known measures of anxiety.

claim: Analyses of the open field revealed no differences between Ccr5+/- mice and their WT controls.
source: Analyses of the open field (e.g., measures of total distance traveled and percentage time in center zone) also revealed no differences between the Ccr5+/- mice and their WT controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the open field test showing no differences in locomotor activity measures.

claim: There is no difference in astrocyte numbers between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in the hippocampus of 3-month old mice.
source: We measured astrocyte numbers and apoptosis with GFAP and TUNEL staining in the hippocampus of 3-month old mice, and found that in our genetic background there is no difference between WT and Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data (GFAP staining) comparing astrocyte numbers in WT and Ccr5+/- mice.

claim: There is no difference in apoptosis between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in the hippocampus of 3-month old mice.
source: We measured astrocyte numbers and apoptosis with GFAP and TUNEL staining in the hippocampus of 3-month old mice, and found that in our genetic background there is no difference between WT and Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data (TUNEL staining) comparing apoptosis in WT and Ccr5+/- mice.

claim: There is no difference in spine density in the hippocampal CA1 subregion between YFP/WT and YFP/Ccr5+/- mice.
source: Measurements of spine density in the hippocampal CA1 subregion revealed no differences between YFP/WT and YFP/Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data comparing spine density in YFP/WT and YFP/Ccr5+/- mice.

claim: The learning and memory enhancements of Ccr5+/- mice are not confounded by abnormal anxiety, changes in locomotor activity, astrogliosis, apoptosis, or spine density.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the learning and memory enhancements of the Ccr5+/- mice are not confounded by abnormal anxiety, changes in locomotor activity, astrogliosis, apoptosis, or spine density.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results from multiple behavioral and histological assays showing no differences in these measures.

claim: Mitogen-activated protein kinases p44/42 (MAPKs) have a central role in hippocampal learning and memory.
source: Mitogen-activated protein kinases p44/42 (MAPKs) (Atkins et al., 1998; Kushner et al., 2005; Schafe et al., 2000) and cAMP-responsive element-binding protein (CREB) (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994) are known to have a central role in hippocampal learning and memory and in cortical plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Atkins et al., 1998; Kushner et al., 2005; Schafe et al., 2000).

claim: cAMP-responsive element-binding protein (CREB) has a central role in hippocampal learning and memory.
source: Mitogen-activated protein kinases p44/42 (MAPKs) (Atkins et al., 1998; Kushner et al., 2005; Schafe et al., 2000) and cAMP-responsive element-binding protein (CREB) (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994) are known to have a central role in hippocampal learning and memory and in cortical plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994).

claim: MAPK and CREB have a central role in cortical plasticity.
source: Mitogen-activated protein kinases p44/42 (MAPKs) (Atkins et al., 1998; Kushner et al., 2005; Schafe et al., 2000) and cAMP-responsive element-binding protein (CREB) (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Dash et al., 1990; Yin et al., 1994) are known to have a central role in hippocampal learning and memory and in cortical plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).

claim: There were no differences between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in hippocampal MAPK activation prior to learning.
source: Prior to learning (measurements in home cage controls), there were no differences between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in either hippocampal MAPK or CREB activation measured with phospho-specific antibodies (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in WT and Ccr5+/- mice under baseline conditions.

claim: There were no differences between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in hippocampal CREB activation prior to learning.
source: Prior to learning (measurements in home cage controls), there were no differences between WT and Ccr5+/- mice in either hippocampal MAPK or CREB activation measured with phospho-specific antibodies (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated CREB levels in WT and Ccr5+/- mice under baseline conditions.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed enhanced phosphorylated MAPK levels at 1 hr after fear conditioning.
source: In contrast, Ccr5+/- mice showed enhanced phosphorylated MAPK (Figure 2B, t(10) = 4.45 p<0.01, Student's t-test) and enhanced phosphorylated CREB levels (Figure 2C, t(12) = 2.21 p<0.05, Student's t-test) at 1 and 3 hr after fear conditioning, respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) of western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in WT and Ccr5+/- mice at 1 hr after training.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed enhanced phosphorylated CREB levels at 3 hr after fear conditioning.
source: In contrast, Ccr5+/- mice showed enhanced phosphorylated MAPK (Figure 2B, t(10) = 4.45 p<0.01, Student's t-test) and enhanced phosphorylated CREB levels (Figure 2C, t(12) = 2.21 p<0.05, Student's t-test) at 1 and 3 hr after fear conditioning, respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of western blot data comparing phosphorylated CREB levels in WT and Ccr5+/- mice at 3 hr after training.

claim: Enhanced MAPK or CREB signaling have been associated with enhancements in learning and memory.
source: Enhanced MAPK or CREB signaling have been associated with enhancements in learning and memory. For example, HRasG12V mice have enhanced MAPK levels following training, and show increases in LTP and sensory plasticity, as well as enhancements in learning and memory tested in a number of tasks (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005); Similarly, enhanced CREB signaling is also associated with memory enhancements in multiple tasks and model systems (Czajkowski et al., 2014; Kathirvelu and Colombo, 2013; Zhou et al., 2009) and in barrel cortex plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing associations between enhanced MAPK/CREB signaling and memory enhancements.

claim: HRasG12V mice have enhanced MAPK levels following training.
source: For example, HRasG12V mice have enhanced MAPK levels following training, and show increases in LTP and sensory plasticity, as well as enhancements in learning and memory tested in a number of tasks (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005).

claim: HRasG12V mice show increases in LTP and sensory plasticity.
source: For example, HRasG12V mice have enhanced MAPK levels following training, and show increases in LTP and sensory plasticity, as well as enhancements in learning and memory tested in a number of tasks (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005).

claim: HRasG12V mice show enhancements in learning and memory tested in a number of tasks.
source: For example, HRasG12V mice have enhanced MAPK levels following training, and show increases in LTP and sensory plasticity, as well as enhancements in learning and memory tested in a number of tasks (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kaneko et al., 2010; Kushner et al., 2005).

claim: Enhanced CREB signaling is associated with memory enhancements in multiple tasks and model systems.
source: Similarly, enhanced CREB signaling is also associated with memory enhancements in multiple tasks and model systems (Czajkowski et al., 2014; Kathirvelu and Colombo, 2013; Zhou et al., 2009) and in barrel cortex plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Czajkowski et al., 2014; Kathirvelu and Colombo, 2013; Zhou et al., 2009).

claim: Enhanced CREB signaling is associated with barrel cortex plasticity.
source: Similarly, enhanced CREB signaling is also associated with memory enhancements in multiple tasks and model systems (Czajkowski et al., 2014; Kathirvelu and Colombo, 2013; Zhou et al., 2009) and in barrel cortex plasticity (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Barth et al., 2000; Glazewski et al., 1999).

claim: Increases in MAPK and CREB signaling are integral to the learning and memory enhancements in the Ccr5 knockout mice.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that increases in MAPK and CREB signaling are integral to the learning and memory enhancements in the Ccr5 knockout mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed increases in MAPK and CREB signaling in Ccr5 knockout mice and the known roles of these pathways in learning and memory.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice show enhanced LTP in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: Analyses of the fEPSPs between 50 and 60 min post-tetanus revealed enhanced LTP in Ccr5+/- mice (Figure 2D, t(12) = 2.61 p<0.05, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.05) of electrophysiological data comparing LTP in WT and Ccr5+/- mice.

claim: The enhancement in MAPK/CREB signaling causes the hippocampal enhancements in LTP that likely underlies the hippocampal-dependent learning and memory enhancements of Ccr5+/- mice.
source: Our results suggest that the enhancement in MAPK/CREB signaling causes the hippocampal enhancements in LTP that likely underlies the hippocampal-dependent learning and memory enhancements of Ccr5+/- mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed enhancements in MAPK/CREB signaling, LTP, and learning and memory in Ccr5+/- mice, and the known roles of these mechanisms.

claim: CCR5 is a plasticity and memory suppressor.
source: More importantly, these signaling, electrophysiological and behavioral results of Ccr5+/- mice suggest that CCR5 is a plasticity and memory suppressor (Abel et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined signaling, electrophysiological, and behavioral results showing enhancements when CCR5 function is reduced, and cites a reference for the concept of memory suppressors.

claim: AAV5 vectors containing shRNA-CCR5 markedly reduced Ccr5 mRNA in the hippocampus one month after injection compared to shRNA-Cont virus.
source: One month after shRNA-CCR5 virus injection, Ccr5 mRNA was markedly reduced in the hippocampus compared to shRNA-Cont virus (Figure 3B, t(7) = 7.54 p<0.001, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.001) of qPCR data comparing Ccr5 mRNA levels in mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 vs. shRNA-Cont AAV.

claim: Infection of shRNA-CCR5, but not shRNA-Cont, reduced Ccr5 expression in cultured HEK293 cells.
source: Similarly, in cultured HEK293 cells, infection of shRNA-CCR5, but not shRNA-Cont reduced Ccr5 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from cultured HEK293 cells showing reduced CCR5 expression with shRNA-CCR5.

claim: GFP expression was observed widely in the hippocampal pyramidal fields one month after shRNA-Cont or shRNA-CCR5 AAV injection.
source: Additionally, one-month after shRNA-Cont or shRNA-CCR5 AAV injection, GFP expression (indicating AAV transfection) was observed widely in the hippocampal pyramidal fields (including CA1 and CA2) of both groups (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing GFP expression in hippocampal pyramidal fields.

claim: Most GFP-positive cells were recognized by the NeuN antibody (neuronal marker), but not by the Iba1 antibody (microglia marker) or the GFAP antibody (astrocyte marker).
source: Most GFP-positive cells were recognized by the NeuN antibody (neuronal marker), but not by the Iba1 antibody (microglia marker) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or the GFAP antibody (astrocyte marker) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that the viral vectors we used mainly transfected neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of GFP with NeuN but not with Iba1 or GFAP.

claim: The viral vectors used mainly transfected neurons in the hippocampus.
source: Most GFP-positive cells were recognized by the NeuN antibody (neuronal marker), but not by the Iba1 antibody (microglia marker) (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or the GFAP antibody (astrocyte marker) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that the viral vectors we used mainly transfected neurons, a result that we also confirmed in the barrel cortex (see results below).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of GFP with neuronal markers but not with glial markers.

claim: shRNA-CCR5 mice showed enhanced contextual memory when tested 2 weeks after training compared to shRNA-Cont mice.
source: When tested 2-weeks after training, the shRNA-CCR5 mice showed enhanced contextual memory compared to shRNA-Cont mice (Figure 3E, t(15) = 3.46 p<0.01, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in mice injected with shRNA-CCR5 vs. shRNA-Cont AAV.

claim: Mice transfected with shRNA-CCR5 virus spent significantly more time in the target quadrant than the other three quadrants in the water maze probe test after 2 days of training.
source: Strikingly, mice transfected with the shRNA-CCR5 virus spent significantly more time in the target quadrant than the other three quadrants [Figure 3F; Two-way ANOVA with repeated measure, overall (virus × percentage of time in each quadrant) interaction: F(3,120) = 4.18; Main effect of quadrant%: F(3,120) = 9.45. Between the target quadrant and all other quadrants for shRNA-CCR5 mice: p<0.001, Bonferroni post-tests; Target quadrant percentage between shRNA-Cont and shRNA-CCR5 group: t(40) = 2.53 p<0.05, Student's t-test].
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests, p<0.001) of water maze probe test data.

claim: Control mice transfected with shRNA-Cont virus failed to learn the water maze task after 2 days of training.
source: Specifically, we utilized the paradigm used for our knockout studies where a probe test was given after 2 days training, when most control mice (transfected with shRNA-Cont virus) still failed to learn the task (e.g., spent similar times in all four quadrants of the maze).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations during the water maze probe test showing that shRNA-Cont mice spent similar times in all quadrants.

claim: With additional training, shRNA-Cont mice are able to show spatial learning in the water maze task.
source: To test whether with more extended training shRNA-Cont mice could also learn the water maze task, a second probe test was given after 5 days of training. In this probe test, both shRNA-Cont and shRNA-CCR5 mice spent more time in the target quadrant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), demonstrating that with additional training the shRNA-Cont mice are able to show spatial learning in the water maze task.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from a second probe test showing that shRNA-Cont mice spent more time in the target quadrant after 5 days of training.

claim: CCR5 is a memory suppressor.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that CCR5 is a memory suppressor and that knocking-down Ccr5 specifically in the adult CA1/CA2 is sufficient to enhance hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined results from viral knockdown experiments showing enhanced learning and memory when Ccr5 is knocked down in adult hippocampus.

claim: Knocking-down Ccr5 specifically in the adult CA1/CA2 is sufficient to enhance hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that CCR5 is a memory suppressor and that knocking-down Ccr5 specifically in the adult CA1/CA2 is sufficient to enhance hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from mice with viral-mediated Ccr5 knockdown in adult hippocampus showing enhanced learning and memory.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice show increases in hippocampal Ccr5 mRNA expression compared to WT mice.
source: Compared to WT mice, CCR5 Tg mice show increases in hippocampal Ccr5 mRNA expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data comparing Ccr5 mRNA levels in CCR5 Tg and WT mice.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice showed robust memory deficits in a context pre-exposure fear-conditioning paradigm.
source: Analyses of a context pre-exposure fear-conditioning paradigm (Matus-Amat et al., 2004) demonstrated that CCR5 Tg mice showed robust memory deficits (Figure 4B, t(26) = 3.71 p=0.001, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.001) of behavioral data comparing contextual fear conditioning in CCR5 Tg and WT mice, and cites a reference for the paradigm.

claim: Only WT mice, but not CCR5 Tg mice, spent more time in the target quadrant than the other three quadrants in the water maze probe test after 3 days of training.
source: In the probe test only WT mice, but not CCR5 Tg mice spent more time in the target quadrant than the other three quadrants [Figure 4C, Two-way ANOVA with repeated measure, Overall (genotype × quadrant%) interaction: F(3,102) = 3.42; Main effect of quadrant%: F(3,102) = 21.44; Between the target quadrant and all other quadrants for WT mice: ***p<0.001, Bonferroni post-tests; Target quadrant percentage between WT and Ccr5 transgenic group: t(34) = 2.33 *p<0.05, Student's t-test].
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests, p<0.001) of water maze probe test data.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice had higher average proximity from the platform and less target platform crossing compared to WT mice in the water maze probe test.
source: CCR5 Tg mice also had higher average proximity from the platform and less target platform crossing compared to WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that CCR5 overexpression results in spatial memory deficits.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the water maze probe test showing higher proximity and fewer platform crossings in CCR5 Tg mice.

claim: CCR5 overexpression results in spatial memory deficits.
source: CCR5 Tg mice also had higher average proximity from the platform and less target platform crossing compared to WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that CCR5 overexpression results in spatial memory deficits.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on behavioral data from the water maze showing impaired performance in CCR5 Tg mice.

claim: With extended training, CCR5 Tg mice also learned the water maze task.
source: When a second probe test was given after extended training, both WT and CCR5 Tg mice spent more time in the target quadrant than the other three quadrants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that with extended training CCR5 Tg mice also learned the water maze task.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from a second probe test showing that CCR5 Tg mice spent more time in the target quadrant after extended training.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice show similar phosphorylated p44/42 MAPK levels to WT controls at baseline or after fear conditioning training.
source: Compared to their WT controls, CCR5 Tg mice show similar phosphorylated p44/42 MAPK levels at baseline or after fear conditioning training (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated MAPK levels in CCR5 Tg and WT mice.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice and their WT controls have similar phosphorylated CREB levels at baseline.
source: Although CCR5 Tg mice and their WT controls have similar phosphorylated CREB levels at baseline (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), CCR5 Tg mice show decreased phospho-CREB levels at 3 hr after fear conditioning training (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated CREB levels in CCR5 Tg and WT mice under baseline conditions.

claim: CCR5 Tg mice show decreased phospho-CREB levels at 3 hr after fear conditioning training.
source: Although CCR5 Tg mice and their WT controls have similar phosphorylated CREB levels at baseline (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), CCR5 Tg mice show decreased phospho-CREB levels at 3 hr after fear conditioning training (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data comparing phosphorylated CREB levels in CCR5 Tg and WT mice at 3 hr after training.

claim: CREB has a critical role in memory consolidation.
source: Because of the critical role of CREB in memory consolidation (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Guzowski and McGaugh, 1997), these results suggest that the memory deficits caused by CCR5 overexpression in excitatory neurons are due to deficits in memory consolidation processes mediated by CREB (Silva et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Guzowski and McGaugh, 1997).

claim: The memory deficits caused by CCR5 overexpression in excitatory neurons are due to deficits in memory consolidation processes mediated by CREB.
source: Because of the critical role of CREB in memory consolidation (Bourtchuladze et al., 1994; Guzowski and McGaugh, 1997), these results suggest that the memory deficits caused by CCR5 overexpression in excitatory neurons are due to deficits in memory consolidation processes mediated by CREB (Silva et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed decrease in phospho-CREB levels in CCR5 Tg mice after training and the known role of CREB in memory consolidation, with citations to supporting studies.

claim: Trimming all whiskers except for D1 produces an increase in the responses of layer 2/3 cells located in deprived barrel-columns to stimulation of the spared D1 whisker.
source: Trimming all of whiskers except for D1 produces both an increase in the responses of layer 2/3 (L2/3) cells located in deprived barrel-columns to stimulation of the spared D1 whisker, and an increase in the size of the spared whisker's representation in the barrel cortex (Fox, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Fox, 1992).

claim: Trimming all whiskers except for D1 produces an increase in the size of the spared whisker's representation in the barrel cortex.
source: Trimming all of whiskers except for D1 produces both an increase in the responses of layer 2/3 (L2/3) cells located in deprived barrel-columns to stimulation of the spared D1 whisker, and an increase in the size of the spared whisker's representation in the barrel cortex (Fox, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Fox, 1992).

claim: 7 days of single whisker experience is insufficient to produce experience-dependent potentiation in WT barrel cortex.
source: Although 7-days of single whisker experience is insufficient to produce experience-dependent potentiation in WT barrel cortex (Glazewski and Fox, 1996), three measures indicated faster potentiation in Ccr5+/- mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Glazewski and Fox, 1996).

claim: Penetrations in barrels surrounding D1 revealed potentiated responses to D1 stimulation in Ccr5+/- but not WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
source: First, penetrations in barrels surrounding D1 revealed potentiated responses to D1 stimulation in Ccr5+/- but not WT mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing potentiated responses in Ccr5+/- mice but not WT mice.

claim: A comparison of each cell's response to the spared versus deprived principal whisker response showed plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice but not in WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
source: Second, a comparison of each cell's response to the spared versus deprived principal whisker response (vibrissae dominance) showed plasticity in Ccr5+/- (Figure 5C, deprived versus undeprived t(21) = 3.222 p<0.01, Student's t-test) but not in WT mice (Figure 5B, deprived versus undeprived, t(11) = 1.663, p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of vibrissae dominance data comparing deprived and undeprived conditions in Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claim: A plot of D1 response versus principal whisker response showed points above the identity line only for Ccr5+/- but not WT mice after 7 days of single whisker experience.
source: Third, a plot of D1 response versus principal whisker (PW) response showed points above the identity line (D1>PW) only for Ccr5+/- but not WT mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by graphical representation of electrophysiology data showing the relationship between D1 and PW responses.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice showed a significant increase in weighted vibrissae dominance index (WVDI) after 7 days deprivation compared to WT mice.
source: Comparison of the time course of vibrissae dominance also showed a significant increase in WVDI in Ccr5+/- mice (0.396 ± 0.051), but not in WT mice (0.111 ± 0.011) after 7 days deprivation [Figure 5E; Interaction: F(2,41) = 1.398, genotype, F(1,41) = 8.919, days deprived F(2,41) = 10.20, genotype and deprivation period are significant: t = 3.05, p<0.05, Bonferroni post-tests].
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA with Bonferroni post-tests, p<0.05) of WVDI data comparing Ccr5+/- and WT mice.

claim: Ccr5+/- mice show faster plasticity in the barrel cortex.
source: These results demonstrate that Ccr5+/- mice show faster plasticity in the barrel cortex.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined electrophysiology data showing enhanced experience-dependent plasticity in Ccr5+/- mice.

claim: A spike-timing dependent protocol induced LTP in 20% of L2/3 cells in WT mice.
source: In WT mice, L2/3 cells showed significant LTP in just 20% of cases while in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice the same protocol produced LTP in 70% of cases (Figure 6B, χ2 = 15.63, p<0.001, χ-squared test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (χ-squared test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data showing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP.

claim: The same spike-timing dependent protocol produced LTP in 70% of L2/3 cells in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice.
source: In WT mice, L2/3 cells showed significant LTP in just 20% of cases while in Ccr5+/- and Ccr5-/- mice the same protocol produced LTP in 70% of cases (Figure 6B, χ2 = 15.63, p<0.001, χ-squared test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (χ-squared test, p<0.001) of in vitro electrophysiology data showing the proportion of cells exhibiting LTP.

claim: WT mice did not show LTP on average with the spike-timing dependent protocol.
